projects.title: Keeping multiple tactile targets distinct
projects.fullTitle: Spatial Tactile Optimizer: Optimizing Perceptual Separability for Multi-Target Vibrotactile Cues on the Torso
projects.alt: Spatial Tactile Optimizer uses a perceptual model and optimization solver to turn fused torso cues into distinct cues for multiple targets.
projects.question: What should a haptic renderer preserve when nearby cues fuse?
projects.summary: STO balances directional fidelity with perceptual separation so multiple simultaneous targets remain distinguishable on the torso.
projects.overview: Presenting each target independently can cause nearby vibrations to fuse into a phantom sensation. STO treats the number of distinct targets as a design requirement, alongside their directions.
projects.system: A model of tactile fusion is incorporated into a mixed-integer optimization problem. A torso-worn array is evaluated in a perceptual study and a first-person game with simultaneous threats.
projects.finding: In the submitted studies, STO improved target-count identification and supported faster responses with fewer unaddressed threats. This benefit came with a bounded displacement of the rendered directions, making the perceptual trade-off explicit.
projects.note: Manuscript under review at CHI 2027. An earlier CHI 2026 extended abstract is listed separately.

projects.title: Giving sound and touch complementary roles
projects.fullTitle: Perceptual Effects of Co-Located Vibrotactile and Auditory Cues on the Head
projects.authors: Dajin Lee, Uison Ju, and Seungmoon Choi
projects.alt: Head-mounted vibration creates tactile and bone-conducted auditory cues, while co-located sound and touch support event identification and localization.
projects.question: When cues share a location, do they need to serve the same purpose?
projects.summary: A head-mounted system examines tactile, bone-conducted, and air-conducted cues, connecting sensory interaction with spatial and semantic tasks.
projects.overview: Vibration on the head can be felt on the skin and heard through bone conduction. Adding spatial sound creates a coupled sensory experience whose channels may contribute differently to a task.
projects.system: A head-mounted vibrotactile system and spatial audio are studied in localization experiments and a virtual task involving direction and event identification. The studies examine both the sound generated by vibration and the contribution of added audio.
projects.finding: The submitted studies suggest complementary task-level roles: tactile feedback helped reduce front–back confusion and elevation error, while sound supported semantic identification. Bone-conducted sound did not significantly impair localization in the tested conditions.
projects.note: Manuscript under review at Virtual Reality (Springer).
projects.extraAlt: Side and top views of the head-mounted display with actuator positions and virtual stimulation locations.
projects.caption: The head-mounted prototype and spatial stimulation locations. Figure from the manuscript under review.

projects.title: Opening up music exploration
projects.fullTitle: Saving More, Choosing Better? Multimodal Music Previews with Text and Vibration
projects.authors: Dajin Lee, Seungmoon Choi, and Oliver Schneider
projects.alt: Multimodal music previews add text and synchronized vibration, with PRISM separating experience, effort, discrimination, and exploration.
projects.question: Does a richer preview help people choose better, or encourage them to explore more?
projects.summary: Text and synchronized vibration reshape short music previews. PRISM separates experiential value and exploration from decision accuracy.
projects.overview: A short excerpt can determine whether an unfamiliar track receives further attention. This project asks how additional sensory and semantic cues change that early encounter, and how its value should be evaluated.
projects.system: Audio, text, vibration, and their combinations are evaluated in a controlled laboratory study with 48 participants and a six-day field deployment with 60 participants. PRISM organizes measures of experience, interaction effort, discrimination, and willingness to explore.
projects.finding: In the submitted studies, richer previews broadened exploration more consistently than they improved discrimination between later-valued and later-rejected tracks. Vibration supported absorption and exploratory listening; text increased perceived sufficiency without a stable gain in discrimination.

projects.title: Aligning sound and touch
projects.fullTitle: Perceptual Alignment of Spatial Auditory and Tactile Stimuli for Effective Directional Cueing
projects.alt: A participant wearing a vibrotactile belt, surrounded by loudspeakers in the spatial alignment experiment.
projects.question: How closely do sound and touch need to align?
projects.summary: Measuring perceptual tolerance to spatial misalignment and using it to inform directional cueing with a sparse tactile array.
projects.overview: Spatial sound and vibration can point toward the same event, but their physical locations do not always match. This work measures how much directional mismatch people can distinguish and tests cueing within those perceptual limits.
projects.system: A vibrotactile belt, spatial sound sources, and an interactive hazard-avoidance task connect psychophysical measurements with an applied cueing system.
projects.finding: Cue alignment within the measured perceptual tolerance supported comparable hazard-avoidance performance and usability to exact physical alignment in the tested conditions.
projects.extraAlt: Overview of measuring directional discrimination and using it to inform tactile actuator placement.
projects.caption: From perceptual measurements to actuator placement and directional cueing. Figure from the published paper.

projects.title: Feeling a virtual object underfoot
projects.fullTitle: Vibrotactile Metaphor of Physical Interaction Using Body-Penetrating Phantom Sensations: Stepping on a Virtual Object
projects.authors: Dajin Lee, Seungjae Oh, Seungmoon Choi, and Bum-Jae You
projects.alt: The foot-worn prototype with labeled actuators on the sole and instep and a pressure sensor.
projects.question: Can vibration evoke the experience of stepping on a virtual object?
projects.summary: A foot-worn interface uses body-penetrating phantom sensations to investigate a vibrotactile metaphor of physical contact.
projects.overview: Coordinated stimulation on the sole and instep can produce a sensation that moves through the foot. This project investigates how that illusion can express contact with a virtual object.
projects.system: A foot-worn vibrotactile prototype is evaluated in passive stimulation and active stepping conditions, with and without visual feedback.
projects.finding: The metaphor was more convincing in passive perception. The benefit was less clear during active stepping, highlighting the importance of the sensations generated by a user's own movement.
projects.extraAlt: Passive seated perception and active stepping experiments with a haptic shoe and visual feedback.
projects.caption: Passive and active experiments. Original author-provided figure from the WHC 2021 paper.

projects.title: Learning physics through force feedback
projects.fullTitle: A Comparative Study of Physical and Haptic Exhibits in an Informal Learning Environment
projects.authors: Dajin Lee, Daehyeon Nam, Jinhyuk Yoon, Dukchan Yoon, Seokwon Jeong, Keehoon Kim, and Seungmoon Choi
projects.alt: A physical lever exhibit beside a large-display virtual exhibit with a cable-driven force-feedback handle.
projects.question: How can a haptic exhibit support hands-on learning?
projects.summary: A cable-driven force-feedback exhibit brings a virtual lever to life and is evaluated alongside a physical science-museum exhibit.
projects.overview: Virtual exhibits offer flexibility, but their value depends on how visitors interact with and learn from them. This study compares a physical lever exhibit with a haptic simulation in a science-museum setting.
projects.system: The collaborative project uses a two-degree-of-freedom cable-driven device, a large visual display, and a virtual lever simulation to present physical interaction.
projects.finding: An observational study with children examined interaction behavior, learning, motivation, and enjoyment, demonstrating the potential of haptic exhibits in informal learning.
projects.extraAlt: Mechanical layout of the cable-driven force-feedback device and large display.
projects.caption: The cable-driven haptic exhibit. Figure from the published paper.

projects.title: HAPTCHA
projects.fullTitle: HAPTCHA: Eyes-Free Haptic CAPTCHA in Mobile Environments: Design Principle, Security Evaluation, and User Experience
projects.authors: Duhong Kweon, Dajin Lee, Seulbae Kim, and Seungmoon Choi
projects.alt: HAPTCHA combines eyes-free mobile interaction while walking with tilt-based orientation search, rhythm reproduction, and two-step human verification.
projects.question: Can touch support eyes-free human verification?
projects.summary: Mobile haptic challenges combine spatial search and rhythm reproduction with evaluation of security and usability during movement.
projects.overview: HAPTCHA explores smartphone vibration as a challenge channel for human verification. It studies the sensorimotor interaction between receiving a tactile cue and responding to it.
projects.system: Two complementary designs use device tilt for spatial search and touch input for rhythm reproduction. Evaluation considers interaction traces as well as usability while sitting and walking.
projects.finding: The study examines both resistance to the evaluated automated attacks and the human effort required to complete the challenges. Security results are specific to the tested threat models.

projects.title: When contact changes intensity
projects.fullTitle: Effects of Contact Force on Vibrotactile Perceived Intensity Across the Upper Body
projects.authors: Dajin Lee, Gyeore Yun, and Seungmoon Choi
projects.alt: A voice-coil actuator and load cell secured to the back of a hand for controlled contact-force measurements.
projects.question: How does the way a wearable touches the body change its feedback?
projects.summary: Characterizing the relationship between contact force, vibration parameters, body location, and perceived intensity.
projects.overview: A wearable's fit affects the force between an actuator and the skin. This work studies how that contact changes the intensity people perceive at the hand, upper arm, and lower back.
projects.system: An actuator and load cell provide controlled stimulation while perceptual magnitude-estimation experiments vary contact force, vibration amplitude, and frequency.
projects.finding: Increasing contact force generally increased perceived intensity, with the pattern depending on body location and stimulation parameters. The results inform more consistent haptic rendering.
projects.note: IEEE Haptics Symposium 2024 Best Paper Award Finalist

projects.title: Giving a tactile illusion meaning through sound
projects.fullTitle: Enhancing Body-Penetrating Phantom Sensations Through Multisensory Integration of Sound and Vibration
projects.authors: Hyunuk Kim, Dajin Lee, and Seungmoon Choi
projects.alt: A torso-mounted vibrotactile arrangement and coordinated sound waveforms for a body-penetrating tactile illusion.
projects.question: How does the meaning of sound change an unfamiliar tactile experience?
projects.summary: Coordinated sound and vibration investigate realism, direction, and user experience in body-penetrating phantom sensations.
projects.overview: An unfamiliar tactile illusion can be interpreted differently depending on its sensory context. This project studies how different sounds shape a body-penetrating phantom sensation.
projects.system: Coordinated vibrotactile stimulation is paired with several sound types, followed by evaluation of perceived realism, directional clarity, satisfaction, and affect.
projects.finding: Penetration-related sounds enhanced perceived realism and satisfaction in the evaluated conditions, illustrating the role of semantic compatibility across modalities.

projects.title: Bringing a museum exhibit back into the story
projects.fullTitle: Augmenting Outdated Museum Exhibits with Embodied and Tangible Interactions for Prolonged Use and Learning Enhancement
projects.authors: Dajin Lee, Daehyeon Nam, and Seungmoon Choi
projects.alt: A virtual blood-flow companion introduces children to an exhibit, then guides a transition to tangible interaction with the physical installation.
projects.question: Can a digital companion draw visitors into a physical exhibit?
projects.summary: Embodied and tangible interactions connect a virtual introduction with hands-on exploration of an existing science-museum exhibit.
projects.overview: Some physical exhibits struggle to attract and retain attention. This project develops a virtual companion that supports interaction before and during use of the original exhibit.
projects.system: A virtual character, embodied interaction, and tangible augmentation create a sequence from initial engagement to hands-on exploration. Iterative development and field evaluation take place in a science museum.
projects.finding: The studies examine visitor engagement, prolonged use, and learning experience, showing how digital augmentation can support interaction with the original physical exhibit.

projects.title: Feeling the rhythm of the body
projects.fullTitle: Modulating Heart Activity and Task Performance Using Haptic Heartbeat Feedback: A Study Across Four Body Placements
projects.authors: Andreia Valente, Dajin Lee, Seungmoon Choi, Mark Billinghurst, and Augusto Esteves
projects.alt: Original UIST 2024 teaser photographs of the haptic heartbeat device worn at the wrist, neck, and ankle.
projects.question: How do the location and rhythm of haptic heartbeat feedback matter?
projects.summary: Studying physiological responses, task performance, and subjective experience across four body placements.
projects.overview: Heartbeat-like haptic feedback connects an external stimulus with the experience of bodily rhythms. This collaborative study investigates how its rhythm and placement affect the response.
projects.system: A vibrotactile system presents heartbeat-like stimulation at the chest, wrist, neck, and ankle while measuring heart activity, task performance, and subjective experience.
projects.finding: The study highlights how physiological measures and subjective preferences can differ across body placements, informing the design of haptic interoceptive feedback.

projects.title: Designing tactile warnings with drivers
projects.fullTitle: Participatory Design for In-Vehicle Vibrotactile Warnings on the Driver’s Seat
projects.authors: Dajin Lee, Jaejun Park, Jeonggoo Kang, Taekun Yun, Dong-Chul Park, and Seungmoon Choi
projects.alt: A driver's seat with multiple vibration actuators and a graphical editor for designing tactile warning patterns.
projects.question: How can drivers help shape the tactile warnings they receive?
projects.summary: A participatory design approach and seat-based haptic platform explore vibrotactile warnings for driving contexts.
projects.overview: Tactile warnings must communicate information while fitting the driver's context and expectations. This work involves participants in the design of seat-based warning patterns.
projects.system: A multi-actuator seat and a visual pattern-design interface support the creation and discussion of vibrotactile warnings.
projects.finding: The participatory process provides design knowledge about how users interpret and construct warning patterns for the driver's seat.

projects.title: Understanding touch in context
projects.fullTitle: Touch with Meaning: A Contextual Analysis of Social Touch
projects.authors: Ayush Bhardwaj, Ashish Pratap, Abbas Khawaja, Yapeng Tian, Uison Ju, Dajin Lee, Seungmoon Choi, and Jin Ryong Kim
projects.alt: Original social-touch teaser showing body-region distributions for affection, comfort, salutation, appreciation, encouragement, inclusion, emphasis, gratitude, playfulness, and dominance.
projects.question: How does context shape the meaning of social touch?
projects.summary: A collaborative analysis of social touch considers the situations and meanings around physical contact.
projects.overview: The same physical contact can take on different meanings depending on the people and situation. This collaborative work examines social touch through its context.
projects.system: The project develops a contextual analysis of social touch. My research internship at the University of Texas at Dallas contributed to the taxonomy development.
projects.finding: The work offers a structured perspective on the context of touch, complementing the perceptual and technical questions in haptic interface design.
